strengths: Addresses a highly relevant and challenging task: reconstructing both dense metric 3D scenes and global human trajectories in the wild from monocular videos.

Proposes an effective joint optimization strategy (JOSH) that utilizes physical contact constraints (contact scale and contact static losses) to bridge and jointly optimize foreground human motion and background scene geometry.

Achieves state-of-the-art results on several challenging datasets (EMDB, SLOPER4D, RICH), significantly outperforming previous methods in global human motion estimation (e.g., reducing error on SLOPER4D by more than 50% compared to WHAM).
Introduces JOSH3R, a fast feedforward alternative (15.4 FPS) trained on automatically generated pseudo-labels from YouTube web videos, demonstrating a scalable training pipeline.
Provides thorough ablation studies for both JOSH and JOSH3R alongside visually compelling qualitative results.
weaknesses: The 2D search heuristic for 3D contact correspondence (finding the closest pixel point in the projected background) does not guarantee 3D proximity. This might introduce incorrect correspondences and noise in scenes with high depth complexity where the human foot projects close to a distant background object.

There is a substantial performance gap between the optimization-based JOSH and the feedforward JOSH3R (e.g., WA-MPJPE100 on SLOPER4D degrades from 148.6 to 271.1), indicating that the real-time model still has significant room for improvement.

The system relies heavily on multiple heavy off-the-shelf models for initialization (MASt3R-SfM, VIMO, VitDet, DEVA, and BSTRO). Cumulative errors or failures in these initializers can negatively impact the final optimization.

strengths: Strong motivation and physically grounded formulation. Jointly optimizing human motion and scene geometry via contact constraints elegantly addresses the scale ambiguity in monocular scene reconstruction while providing realistic groundings for human movements.

State-of-the-art performance across multiple challenging benchmarks. JOSH outperforms recent competitive methods (such as WHAM, SLAHMR, and TRAM) by a large margin on global human motion estimation (e.g., on EMDB, SLOPER4D, and RICH) and shows superior dense scene reconstruction quality.

Practical dual-contribution design. The paper proposes both a high-accuracy joint optimization framework (JOSH) and a real-time, optimization-free model (JOSH3R) that can run at 15.4 FPS. Training JOSH3R on pseudo-labels generated by JOSH shows a great path forward for data-driven global HMR models.
Thorough evaluation and ablations. Comprehensive ablation studies are provided for both the optimization components in JOSH and the architectural features in JOSH3R, validating each design decision.
Excellent presentation. The manuscript is well-written, structurally sound, and supported by highly informative diagrams and qualitative results.
weaknesses: High sensitivity to initializations. Because JOSH relies on a complex pipeline of external models (MASt3R for scene, VIMO/TRAM for human pose, and BSTRO for contact labels) for initialization, poor performance or errors in any of these modules (especially noisy contact predictions) can lead the optimization to local minima. The paper would be stronger with a robustness analysis on noisy contact labels.

Significant performance gap between JOSH and JOSH3R. Although JOSH3R is designed to handle large-scale web videos in real-time, its reconstruction accuracy is much lower than JOSH (e.g., WA-MPJPE of 271.1 vs 120.0 on SLOPER4D).

Assumption of static backgrounds. The dense scene reconstruction assumes a static background. Dynamic objects other than the tracked humans (such as moving vehicles or wind-blown vegetation) could degrade the robustness of background point cloud trimming and alignment.

Lack of visual failure analysis. Although limitations are discussed, the paper would benefit from a visual presentation of failure modes (e.g., when severe self-occlusions occur or when contacts are wrongly detected) to better understand the boundaries of the method.

strengths: The paper addresses a very challenging and highly relevant task: joint 4D human-scene reconstruction from monocular in-the-wild videos, resolving both camera motion, scene structure on a metric scale, and global human trajectories.

The proposed joint optimization method, JOSH, achieves impressive, state-of-the-art results on several challenging benchmarks (EMDB, SLOPER4D, and RICH) for both global human motion estimation and dense scene reconstruction.

The introduction of JOSH3R—an end-to-end, real-time variant trained using pseudo-labels generated by the optimization pipeline—is a practical and valuable contribution that demonstrates how the heavy optimization pipeline can bootstrap efficient neural estimators.
The ablation studies are thorough and systematically show the influence of each component (e.g., contact scale loss, contact static loss, and optimization of human parameters).
The paper is very well-written, with highly descriptive figures (such as the pipeline overview and qualitative results) and clear mathematical formulations.
weaknesses: The core concept of using contact constraints to align human motion and scene reconstruction is somewhat similar to prior works like SLAHMR, meaning the conceptual novelty is slightly incremental, although the integration with modern dense SfM models (MASt3R) is executed very successfully.

The pipeline relies heavily on multiple complex off-the-shelf networks (DEVA for segmentation, VIMO/SMPLer-X for human mesh recovery, BSTRO for contact estimation, and MASt3R). A failure in any of these upfront estimators could easily cascade into the joint optimization, and a robustness analysis on noisy contact/initializations is missing.

There is a substantial performance gap between the optimization-based JOSH and the fast end-to-end JOSH3R (e.g., WA-MPJPE100 on SLOPER4D drops from 148.6 to 271.1). While JOSH3R is much faster, its accuracy remains significantly lower.

strengths: Joint Optimization Framework: Instead of relying on traditional sequential pipelines, JOSH proposes a unified, single-stage framework that jointly optimizes dense scene reconstruction, camera poses, and multi-human global motion, allowing them to mutually regularize and improve one another.

Physical Grounding via Contact Constraints: The introduction of contact scene loss ($L_{c1}$) and contact static loss ($L_{c2}$) acts as a strong physical and geometric bridge between the human and the scene. This effectively resolves metric scale ambiguities and significantly improves physical plausibility metrics (e.g., reducing foot sliding and floating).

Scalability and Bootstrapping: The paper demonstrates the practical utility of JOSH by using it to generate pseudo-labels on 20 hours of unannotated web videos. Training an end-to-end model (JOSH3R) on this data yields substantial performance gains, showcasing a promising path for scaling up future models.

Extensive and Convincing Evaluation: The method is rigorously evaluated on multiple challenging datasets (SLOPER4D, EMDB, RICH) across several metrics (pose accuracy, depth estimation, chamfer distance, and physical plausibility), demonstrating consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines.
weaknesses: Computational Complexity: The joint optimization framework JOSH is computationally heavy, running at only 0.8 FPS. Although the end-to-end model JOSH3R achieves real-time speeds (15.4 FPS), its reconstruction accuracy drops significantly compared to the optimization pipeline.

Heuristic Contact Matching: The contact scene loss ($L_{c1}$) relies on a heuristic nearest-neighbor search in the 2D projected space combined with monocular depth filtering. This heuristic might be prone to incorrect associations in crowded scenes or complex background geometries.

Sensitivity to Initialization: As a gradient-based optimization method, JOSH's final convergence is heavily dependent on the quality of the initial estimates (local SMPL parameters, depths, etc.) provided by off-the-shelf models. If these initializations contain massive errors, the optimization might fall into poor local minima.

strengths: Proposes JOSH, a novel single-stage joint optimization framework that simultaneously refines camera poses, dense 3D scene point clouds, and global 4D human motion, effectively exploiting the natural synergy between humans and their environments.

Introduces physically-grounded contact constraints (Contact Scene Loss and Contact Static Loss) to guide the joint optimization, leading to highly coherent human-scene interactions with significantly reduced foot-sliding and floating.
Successfully addresses the scale/depth-focal-length ambiguity in monocular videos by dynamically optimizing camera intrinsics alongside human-scene parameters.
Provides extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations on multiple public benchmarks (SLOPER4D, EMDB, RICH) demonstrating clear improvements over state-of-the-art sequential pipelines.

Demonstrates the scalability of the method by using JOSH to pseudo-label 20 hours of web videos, which facilitates the training of a real-time (15.4 FPS) end-to-end feed-forward model (JOSH3R) with strong generalization capabilities.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on off-the-shelf initialization models (e.g., for local human mesh recovery, contact prediction, tracking). Catastrophic failures in these initial steps (e.g., under severe occlusion) can cause the optimization to get stuck in poor local minima.
High computational complexity of the offline optimization process (running at 0.8 FPS), which limits its direct applicability for real-time or online scenarios.

The contact point correspondence heuristic (L_c1) relies on 2D projection and monocular depth filtering. While robust for ground contacts, it may face difficulties in highly complex multi-contact scenarios (e.g., hands interacting with intricate geometries or thin objects).

The joint objective function involves multiple loss terms and hyperparameters, which could require careful tuning when adapting the framework to completely different environments or motion distributions.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly challenging and important problem: 4D human-scene reconstruction from monocular, in-the-wild videos.
The proposed single-stage joint optimization framework (JOSH) successfully bridges camera, human, and scene reconstruction, allowing mutual refinement through physical contact constraints.

The quantitative results across three distinct datasets (SLOPER4D, EMDB, RICH) show clear improvements in global human motion estimation, dense scene reconstruction, and physics plausibility compared to sequential pipelines.
The paper demonstrates the practical potential of using JOSH for scalable pseudo-labeling on unstructured web videos to train feed-forward models.
weaknesses: The conceptual and algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited. The framework relies heavily on a complex pipeline of multiple off-the-shelf models (DEVA for segmentation, BSTRO for contact estimation, HMR2.0/WHAM/VIMO for humans, MASt3R for scene initialization) and optimizes them using standard loss formulations (reprojection, temporal smoothness, contact distance). It reads more like a solid system-engineering effort than a fundamental algorithmic contribution.
The optimization-based version (JOSH3) is computationally expensive, running at only 0.8 FPS. This severely restricts its practical application to offline preprocessing.

To address the speed limitation, the authors introduce JOSH3R, but its performance degrades drastically compared to JOSH3 (e.g., WA-MPJPE on SLOPER4D drops from 120.0 to 296.3, and W-MPJPE from 438.3 to 1148.4). In fact, JOSH3R's accuracy is worse than some existing baseline methods like WHAM (which achieves 297.7 on SLOPER4D compared to JOSH3R's 296.3 and has much better W-MPJPE), undermining the practicality of the real-time model.

The monocular optimization of camera intrinsics (focal length), extrinsic poses, per-pixel dense depths, and multi-human scales is highly under-constrained. The mechanism used to resolve the fundamental depth-scale-focal-length ambiguity during joint optimization is not rigorously analyzed or explained, raising concerns about optimization stability on arbitrary videos.

As acknowledged in the limitations, the optimization is highly sensitive to the initializations. If the initial off-the-shelf predictions are of poor quality (e.g., under heavy occlusion or challenging lighting), the joint optimization is prone to getting stuck in bad local minima.
